analysis.one_liner: Requires social media, gaming, and streaming apps to protect minors by default and opens their data to independent researchers.
analysis.headline: 72 senators cosponsored the bill and it cleared the Senate Commerce Committee, but it never got a final vote in the Senate or the House before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required social media, gaming, and streaming apps likely used by people under 17 to run with safety protections switched on by default: limits on features built to stretch use, controls over algorithmic recommendations, and tools for parents, with the most protective privacy settings pre-set for kids. It would have banned ads for tobacco, alcohol, gambling, and drugs aimed at minors, restricted ads targeted at them using their personal data, and forced large platforms to publish yearly independent audits of the risks their products pose to children. It would also have given approved researchers access to platform data to study harms, and enforcement would have sat with the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general, including lawsuits seeking damages.
analysis.who_benefits: Parents and everyone under 17 who uses social media, streaming, or gaming apps. They would have gotten protective settings on by default, opt-outs from algorithmic recommendation feeds and targeted advertising, tools to report harms with response deadlines, and bans on ads for tobacco, alcohol, gambling, and drugs aimed at minors. Independent researchers would have gained a formal program to access platform data, and state attorneys general would have gained the power to sue platforms on behalf of residents and win damages.

how_it_helps.text: Platforms would owe a duty of care to minors: reasonable design measures to prevent and mitigate anxiety, depression, eating disorders, suicidal behavior, addiction-like usage patterns, bullying, sexual exploitation, and marketing of drugs, tobacco, gambling, or alcohol to minors.

Minors would get safeguards on the most protective default setting: limits on communication from strangers, restrictions on public personal data, controls over features like autoplay and notifications that extend use, opt-outs from personalized recommendation systems, and restrictions on geolocation sharing.

Parents would get tools to view and (for children under 13) control a minor's privacy and account settings, restrict purchases, and see and cap time spent, and platforms would need verifiable parental consent before a child under 13 starts using one.

Platforms would have to stop facilitating ads for age-restricted products like tobacco and gambling to minors, label ads and paid endorsements, and, in the committee-approved version, stop directing individual-specific advertising to minors based on their personal data or cross-site tracking.
Platforms with more than 10 million U.S. monthly users would face an annual public report on risks to minors based on an independent third-party audit, with access to the platform's systems and data.

A federal program would let approved university and nonprofit researchers access platform data to study harms to minors, and the committee-approved version would require large platforms to offer users a version of the service that does not prioritize content using their personal data.
Violations would be enforceable by the FTC and by state attorneys general, who could sue to stop practices and obtain damages, restitution, or other compensation for residents.

analysis.who_pays: The largest social media, streaming, and gaming companies: they would have redesigned products around a legal duty to minors, submitted to yearly independent audits, provided data to approved researchers, and faced enforcement suits from the FTC and state attorneys general. Teens themselves would carry a trade-off cost: the same bill hands parents visibility into their privacy and account settings, which functions as monitoring.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large social media and gaming platforms

drawbacks.text: The bill requires platforms to give parents tools to view a minor's privacy and account settings and to notify minors when parental tools are in effect. For teenagers, these are monitoring tools, and they do the most damage when the parent is the source of the problem.

The duty of care requires 'reasonable measures' to prevent and mitigate harms like anxiety and addiction-like use without defining which measures qualify. The bill says it does not require age gating or verification, but platforms facing this duty would still have to decide who counts as a minor, likely by inferring or collecting more age data than they do today.

Because the duty of care covers broad harms such as anxiety and depression, the cheapest way for a platform to comply may be to wall minors off from content and features rather than change the recommendation systems and business incentives the bill targets.

The research program lets platforms require nondisclosure agreements from approved researchers as a condition of data access, though the agreements cannot restrict publishing findings, and platforms can appeal data requests on privacy and security grounds.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill is its strongest part: protective settings on by default, genuine opt-outs from algorithmic feeds and targeted ads, ad restrictions on age-restricted products, yearly outside audits of risk to minors, and real enforcement through the FTC and state attorneys general. The costs are real but secondary: the vague duty of care could push platforms toward restricting what minors can see instead of fixing design incentives, and the mandated parental tools give parents a window into teenagers' accounts that some teens will find invasive. On balance the bill would have shifted power over minors' online experience from platform design teams to families, and made platform practices toward kids public and enforceable.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the Senate Commerce Committee and sat on the Senate calendar with 72 cosponsors, but it never came to a final vote in the Senate and never got a House vote before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Blumenthal introduced the bill on May 2, 2023 with a broad bipartisan list of original cosponsors including Senator Marsha Blackburn, and it was referred to the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee.
The committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute on July 27, 2023, and reported it to the Senate with amendments on December 13, 2023.

The committee-approved version added requirements that large websites offer users notice of personalization algorithms and a non-personalized version of the service, and added a National Academy of Sciences study of harms to minors from social media.
After being reported, the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 287), where bills wait for floor time.
The bill gathered 72 Senate cosponsors: 36 of 49 Republicans, 35 of 48 Democrats, and 1 of 4 independents.
The action history ends at the calendar placement; the bill never received a Senate floor vote or a House vote, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without the bill becoming law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest social media and video-streaming companies. The bill would have imposed a legal duty to design their products around minors' safety, yearly independent audits of the risks their products pose to children, limits on targeted advertising to minors, and lawsuits from the FTC and state attorneys general. None of that took effect, so their engagement-and-ads business model toward young users was left as it was.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and built a bipartisan cosponsor coalition of 72 senators.

for.name: Sen. Maria Cantwell
for.role: Chair, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill favorably out of committee with amendments on December 13, 2023 and placed it on the Senate calendar.

for.name: Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill to the Senate floor in July 2024, where senators voted 86-1 on a procedural step to advance it, though no final vote followed.

for.name: Sen. Marsha Blackburn
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor who carried the bill's bipartisan pairing on the Republican side.

against.name: Mike Johnson
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill or its House companion to the House floor for a vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Postponed the committee's September 2024 markup of the House companion bill after members announced objections; the House never voted on it.

against.name: Thomas Massie
against.what_they_did: Announced opposition to the House companion at the scheduled markup, contributing to its postponement.

against.name: Ken Buck
against.what_they_did: Announced opposition to the House companion at the scheduled markup, contributing to its postponement.

against.name: NetChoice
against.role: Tech industry trade group for large platforms including Meta, Google, TikTok, and X
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against the bill and its state-level versions, arguing it would force online censorship and burden platforms.

against.name: Electronic Frontier Foundation and ACLU
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill publicly, arguing the parental monitoring tools and vague duty of care would threaten young users' privacy and free expression.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship split nearly evenly across parties — 36 of 49 Senate Republicans, 35 of 48 Senate Democrats, and 1 of 4 independents cosponsored — and the main resistance came from House Republican leaders declining to schedule a vote, tech industry lobbying, and civil-liberties objections rather than from either party's caucus.

industries.industry: Large social media platforms (Meta, Google/YouTube, TikTok, Snap, X)
industries.note: The bill would impose a duty to design around minors' safety, protective defaults, annual third-party audits, data access for researchers, and FTC and state lawsuits. The engagement features and targeted advertising that drive their revenue are exactly what the bill targets.

The committee version would bar directing individual-specific advertising to minors based on their personal data, psychological profiling, or cross-site tracking, and would require labels explaining why a minor is seeing an ad. Advertising built on minors' data is the direct subject of the restriction.

industries.industry: Online video game and streaming companies
industries.note: Online video games with chat, user uploads, or microtransactions, and video streaming services, count as covered platforms and would owe the same duty of care, safeguards, and parental tools as social networks.

industries.industry: Smaller platforms under 10 million U.S. users
industries.note: Platforms below the 10-million-user threshold are exempt from the annual independent audit, the research data-access program, and the transparency reporting, so large rivals bear compliance costs they do not.
A new program would give approved university and nonprofit researchers access to platform datasets to study harms to minors, ending their current dependence on platforms' willingness to share data.
